title: Idempotency Keys Under Distributed Retry Pressure: Key Scoping, Storage Contracts, and the Deduplication Boundary
description: How idempotency keys fail in production: scoping mistakes, storage race conditions, TTL traps, and the deduplication boundary every retry path crosses.
linkedin_post:
Idempotency keys are one of those patterns that look solved on a whiteboard and break in production in surprisingly specific ways.

The failure modes are not in the concept. They are in the mechanics:

— Key scoping that is too broad causes false deduplication across tenants or operations
— Redis as the idempotency store without noeviction silently drops records under memory pressure
— Treating a Pending record the same as a missing record allows concurrent execution of the same logical operation
— TTL that is undocumented leaves callers guessing about their retry window
— Response caching across schema changes returns unparseable shapes during rolling deployments

The core constraint most implementations miss: the idempotency record must commit in the same atomic scope as the side effect. If you write the key to Redis and the business record to MongoDB in separate operations, you have a probabilistic guarantee, not a real one.

The transactional approach — writing the idempotency document inside the same MongoDB multi-document transaction as the business record — gives you an atomic check-and-set via duplicate key detection, without a separate two-phase commit protocol.

The Pending state is a correctness boundary, not an edge case. A second request that arrives while a first is in-flight must not proceed. And a Pending record that is older than your request timeout chain must be reaped by a background process before a retry is allowed to claim the key.
